title: Reading & Use of English
paragraphs: Nine months ago, Kamila could say only three things in English: "Hello", "Thank you", and "Goodbye." She knew the alphabet and a few numbers, but she could not hold a conversation, read a paragraph, or write a single sentence. Today, she is sitting at her desk, preparing for the A1.1 Final Exam, and she feels a mixture of nervousness and pride.

Looking back, Kamila remembers the moment everything changed. In the early modules, she learned the Present Simple tense — how to describe daily routines, facts, and habits. She discovered that third-person singular verbs take an -s ending: "She studies every morning", "He reads the news." This one discovery opened the door to describing the world around her.

The biggest challenge came when Kamila first encountered conditional sentences. Zero conditionals — "If you heat water to 100°C, it boils" — were straightforward, but the first conditional — "If I study hard, I will pass the exam" — felt more personal. It expressed real possibilities in her own life. She repeated this structure hundreds of times until it became natural.

Grammar was not the only challenge. One important module introduced vocabulary about work and careers, and Kamila discovered that English uses very specific collocations: you "apply for" a job, you "get" a promotion, you "make" progress, you "take" responsibility. These were not rules she could guess — she had to memorise them carefully.

The passive voice transformed the way Kamila thought about sentences. Instead of always thinking about who does the action, she could now describe results and processes: "The exam was written by the teacher", "The results will be announced next week", "Kazakh is spoken by millions of people." This skill felt especially useful for academic and professional contexts.

Perhaps the most elegant structure Kamila learned was the relative clause. Sentences like "She is a student who never gives up" or "English is a language that connects people worldwide" allowed her to combine ideas and express complex thoughts in a single sentence. As Kamila reads through her notes one last time before the exam, she feels ready. She has come a long way from "Hello, thank you, goodbye."

vocab.example: "Make progress" is a collocation — you cannot say "do progress."

task1Items.question: If you heat water to 100°C, it ___ . (zero conditional — present tense result)
If I study hard, I ___ the exam. (first conditional — will + base)
The exam ___ by the teacher last week. (passive — past simple)
Kazakh ___ by millions of people in Central Asia. (passive — present simple)
She is a student ___ never gives up. (relative clause — person)
Kamila ___ a job at a translation company last spring. (collocation: apply for)
I ___ every collocation in my notebook this semester. (present perfect)
She started ___ progress after the first month of study. (verb + -ing)
It is a good habit ___ your notes every evening. (infinitive of purpose)
By the end of the course, she realised she ___ harder than ever before. (past perfect)

task2Items.statement: Before the course, Kamila could hold a basic English conversation.
Learning the -s ending for third-person verbs helped Kamila describe the world around her.
Kamila found zero conditionals harder than first conditionals.

Kamila guessed the rules for collocations without memorising them.
